case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.limits: The camera captured a scene a human staged in full. A generative model contributes expressive choices of its own, and how much human selection is enough is exactly what the Copyright Office and the courts are now drawing case by case.
case.holding: A photograph can be copyrighted because the photographer's choices of pose, lighting, arrangement and expression make the human, not the camera, the author of the work.

live_cases.name: University of Tennessee Research Foundation v. Anthropic PBC

case.why_ai_cites_it: The first machine-authorship case, and the template both sides use. AI companies and their users cite it for the claim that prompting, curating and arranging make a human the author of machine-assisted output; opponents cite it for the premise that authorship requires a human making the creative choices at all.

reading.body:
The Supreme Court's 1884 ruling in *Burrow-Giles* established that authorship belongs to the human who makes expressive choices, not to the instrument that executes them, and that premise is now the central axis of AI copyright litigation.

The holding was narrow and specific: a photographer who arranged a subject's pose, lighting, and expression was the author of the resulting photograph, because those choices were his, not the camera's. Both sides of current AI disputes reach back to this logic. AI companies and their users argue that prompting, selecting, and curating output satisfies the same standard. Opponents argue that the ruling's premise, that a human must make the creative choices, is precisely what generative models undermine, because the model itself contributes expressive decisions that no human dictated.

The data identifies one live case connected to this precedent, *University of Tennessee Research Foundation v. Anthropic PBC*, which signals that the doctrine is actively in play rather than settled. What the data does not cover is how courts or the Copyright Office are resolving the threshold question the case record flags directly: how much human selection is enough when a generative model is also making choices. That question is being drawn case by case, and *Burrow-Giles* supplies the frame without supplying the answer.
